context: The horizontal axis shows product prices, labeled 0, 3, 10, 25, 80, 200, and +∞ from left to right. The vertical axis shows probability density, with ticks from 0.0 to 0.4. The gray bell-shaped curve peaks near a price of 25. It illustrates the shape of the distribution. The figure gives neither the distribution parameters nor exact bucket probabilities.
description: The horizontal axis is schematic and nonlinear. For example, the price difference from 0 to 3 is 3, and the difference from 80 to 200 is 120, but the horizontal distances in pixels are not proportional to those differences. The apparent bucket widths therefore do not give the actual price spans, and measuring the area under the displayed curve cannot yield exact bucket probabilities.

The six braces below the curve correspond to the six buckets in the table. The rightmost bucket has no finite upper bound. The aim is to use interval probabilities from the actual distribution to give each bucket roughly the same expected number of data points. The figure does not give exact probabilities or establish that the six probabilities are identical.

frames.explanation: The label <3 excludes 3, and >200 excludes 200. Middle labels such as 3–10 leave endpoint inclusion unspecified. If the six buckets cover the entire price range, 3 must belong to the second bucket and 200 to the fifth. This follows from the coverage requirement. The figure does not give a complete endpoint rule, so an implementation must specify where shared boundaries such as 10, 25, and 80 belong.
frames.title: Choosing bucket ranges from a price distribution

summary: Choose boundaries using the distribution of product prices so that data points have roughly equal chances of falling into each bucket. This keeps the data from crowding into just a few buckets.
